'''Thomas Arnot Lumsden''' was a Scottish mathematician, who was educated at the [[University of Edinburgh]], and lectured at [[Birmingham University]]. He published "A certain type of Fourier-Bessel Series", a paper about Bessel functions, in 1924. Lumsden, who served during both [[World War I]] (1914–1918) and [[World War II]] (1941–1945), was killed in action in 1944.

== Personal life, education, and World War I ==
Thomas Lumsden was born on 19 September 1895 in Edinburgh, to Mary Scott Arnott, who was born in [[Glasgow]] in 1857, and William Lumsden, a wood turner born in 1858 in [[Penicuik]], Scotland. He had an older sister, Janet (1889-1935), and younger brother, Andrew (born in 1898).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Thomas Lumsden - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Lumsden/ |access-date=2023-07-04 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

Lumsden started studying at George Heriot's in 1906, a private school in Edinburgh.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our School - George Heriot's - tagline or similar here |url=https://www.george-heriots.com/our-school/ |access-date=2023-07-05 |website=George Heriot's School |language=en-GB}}</ref>{{efn|In April 1911, he passed the leaving certificate and the Edinburgh University Preliminary Examinations in Latin at the lower level, and English at the higher level. In April 1912, he passed Mathematics at Higher Level, then passed Dynamics and Science at Higher level in September 1912.}} He matriculated at the University of Edinburgh in October 1912.{{efn|Lumsden first studied Mathematics, Natural Philosophy and chemistry at Edinburgh University. Following that he studied Political economics before starting his honours course in Mathematics and Natural Philosophy in his 1914-1915 session. During this session, he was ranked second top student and awarded a First Class Certificate in the advanced honours class in Mathematics in June 1915.}}

Lumsden took a break from his studies to fight in [[World War I]] where he was assigned to a Special Brigade of the [[Royal Engineers]]. He was a corporal from July 1915 to April 1917. Lumsden worked then in Munitions until December 1918.<ref name="Roll of Honour">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=azIPAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA441 |title=University of Edinburgh Roll of Honour 1914-1919 |date=1921 |publisher=University of Edinburgh |pages=441 |language=en}}</ref> Lumsden was awarded a BSc in absentia on 5 July 1917.<ref name="EUC">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9wALAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA655|title=The Edinburgh University Calendar |date=1917 |publisher=University of Edinburgh |pages=655 |language=en}}</ref> He returned from his service in 1918 to continue his studies at the University of Edinburgh, graduating with honours for his master's degree in 1919.<ref name="Roll of Honour" />

On 4 August 1924, Lumsden married Florence Milne Falconer in [[Abernyte]], [[Perthshire]].<ref name=":0" /> Their only child, William Fairly Lumsden was born on 6 February 1926.<ref>{{citation|title=England & Wales, Civil Registration Birth Index, 1916-2007 }}</ref>{{efn|Thomas and Florence Lumsden are listed in the 1939 England and Wales register, Thomas' occupation is listed as "University lecturer mathematics",<ref>{{citation|title=1939 England and Wales Register }}</ref> and their address is listed as Hallewell Road, which was the same address later as the residence of his wife when he died.}}

==Career==
Between 1919-1920, Lumsden remained at the University of Edinburgh as an Assistant in Natural Philosophy (under the Nichol Foundation). Following this, he moved to Birmingham to take a position as a lecturer in mathematics at [[University of Birmingham]].

In 1922, he was elected as a Fellow of the [[Royal Astronomical Society]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JD80AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA392 |title=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |date=1922 |publisher=Priestley and Weale |page=392 |language=en}}</ref> In 1922, Lumsden helped [[G. N. Watson]], a mathematics professor at the University of Birmingham, publish a book on [[Bessel function]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |first1=G. N. | last1= Watson |title= A Treatise On The Theory Of Bessel Functions {{!}} PDF  |url=https://www.scribd.com/document/363831446/194797323-Watson-ATreatiseOnTheTheoryOfBesselFunctions-Text-pdf |access-date=2023-07-21 |website=Scribd |language=en}}</ref> Lumsden later published his own paper on Bessel functions in 1924, titled: "A certain type of Fourier-Bessel Series".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lumsden |first=T. A. |date=1924 |title=A Certain Type of Fourier-Bessel Series |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/plms/s2-22.1.381 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s2-22 |issue=1 |pages=381–388 |doi=10.1112/plms/s2-22.1.381|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This paper was cited in [[Thomas John I'Anson Bromwich]]'s book, "An Introduction to The Theory of Infinite Series" in 1926.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bromwich T J I A |url=http://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.163740 |title=An Introduction To The Theory Of Infinite Series Second Edition |last2=Iisc |date=1926 |publisher=Macmillan and Co Ltd}}</ref>

==World War II==
During [[World War II]] (1941–1945), Lumsden once again served his country. He arrived in [[New York City]] on the [[RMS Queen Elizabeth|RMS ''Queen Elizabeth'']] on 26 December 1942, intending to stay indefinitely, but no intention to become a citizen.<ref>{{citation |title=Thomas Arnot Lumsden, born in Edinburg about 1895, had lived in Birmingham with his wife when he left for the United States | work=Arriving Passenger and Crew Lists (including Castle Garden and Ellis Island), 1820-1957 | publisher=The National Archives and Records Administration |location=Washington, D.C.|via=ancestry.com}}</ref> He was identified as a government official and a diplomat.

Lumsden was killed in action on 17 August 1944.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tdUXAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA128 |title=University of Edinburgh Journal |date=1945 |publisher=University of Edinburgh |page=128 |language=en}}</ref>
